extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students and general readers of American government and constitutional history
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted principles and standards implied and stated in a textbook account of the movement to replace the Articles of Confederation and draft the Federal Constitution. Focuses on the functional requirements, procedural choices, and political safeguards the framers regarded as necessary for a viable national government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate_central_taxation_and_revenue_power
rubrics_metrics.description: The national government must have reliable sources of revenue and the power to raise and collect funds so that reliance on irregular requisitions will not 'hazard ... the existence of the Union.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text argues that requisitions under the Articles were ineffective (Congress laid over $10,000,000 in requisitions and received less than one-fourth) and that a 'general revenue' was necessary to maintain public faith at home and abroad. The framers inserted clauses in the Constitution forbidding states to defeat national revenue by issuing competing currency or impairing contracts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power_to_regulate_and_enforce_commerce_and_treaties
rubrics_metrics.description: The national government must be able to regulate foreign commerce and enforce treaty stipulations against unwilling or recalcitrant states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under the Articles Congress could make treaties but could not enforce treaty stipulations on states that regulated commerce in their own way; states laid duties, bid against one another, and interfered with national commercial policy. The Constitution should remedy this inability to secure treaty and commercial obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevention_of_interstate_commercial_conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: A constitutional framework should prevent states from engaging in commercial warfare (discriminatory tariffs, duties, and entry fees) that undermines national economic cooperation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: New York imposing duties and entry fees on Connecticut and New Jersey trade, retaliation by states, and states 'making commercial war upon one another' illustrate the need for national regulation to secure mutual economic advantages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monetary_stability_and_prohibition_on_state_issuance_of_paper_money
rubrics_metrics.description: Constitutional provisions should forbid states from emitting bills of credit or making anything but gold and silver legal tender, to prevent depreciation of currency and impairment of contracts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text documents rampant depreciation of paper money during and after the Revolution (a paper dollar worth less than two cents in specie in 1780) and the Rhode Island conflict where state-issued paper collapsed in value. Framers therefore forbade state issuance of bills of credit and laws impairing contract obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability_to_maintain_public_order_and_respond_to_insurrections
rubrics_metrics.description: The national government must be capable of assisting states and preserving public order when internal violence threatens duly constituted authorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shays' Rebellion is cited as evidence that 'grave dangers to public order' might arise and that the inability to secure assistance from neighboring states or a federal authority could allow the overthrow of state governments by violence — justifying federal capacity to act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement_authority_over_states_or_mechanisms_to_secure_state_obedience
rubrics_metrics.description: A national government should not be 'destitute even of a shadow of a constitutional power to enforce the execution of its own laws' — it needs express powers to exact obedience or punish recalcitrant states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under the Articles, Congress depended on states for enforcement and had no express power to punish or coerce. Framers sought to correct this impotence so national measures could be effectively executed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislation_applicable_to_individuals_rather_than_only_states
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid the principle of legislating solely for states as corporate entities; national legislation should reach individuals so Congress can bring pressure to bear on matters (e.g., taxation, manpower) that ultimately depend on individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton criticized the 'great and radical vice' of legislation for states in their corporate capacity, which left Congress unable to exert pressure on individuals and made enforcement impracticable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical_amendment_and_ratifcation_rules_to_enable_effective_change
rubrics_metrics.description: Constitutional design should include realistic rules for implementation and amendment that do not require unanimous consent and thus avoid deadlock.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convention delegates provided that the new government would go into effect when ratified by nine states (rather than unanimous approval required by the Articles), a deliberate procedural choice to ensure feasibility of establishing the new system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation_of_powers:_legislative_executive_judiciary
rubrics_metrics.description: A national government ought to be established consisting of a supreme legislative, executive, and judiciary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On May 30, 1787 the Committee of the Whole adopted this resolution. The tripartite structure was presented as foundational to a 'national' government with 'complete and compulsive operation.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Supremacy_and_compulsive_operation_of_national_government_over_compact_theory
rubrics_metrics.description: The national government should be more than a mere compact resting on goodwill; it must possess supremacy and the ability to operate compulsively where necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gouverneur Morris contrasted a federal 'compact' with a national government that has 'complete and compulsive operation,' arguing that in all communities there must be one supreme power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checks_and_balances_to_protect_private_property_and_minority_rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Design the government to safeguard the rights of private property and the interests of minorities against the 'superior force' of interested majorities and levelling tendencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convention debates (Madison, Morris, Hamilton, others) framed property protection as a principal object of government; checks and balances, bicameralism with a Senate protecting minority/property interests, and other structural safeguards were advanced to that end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balancing_strength_with_safeguards_against_despotism_and_majority_oppression
rubrics_metrics.description: The system should be stable and efficient (capable of defending the nation, paying debts, and guaranteeing rights) while also checking both the possibility of despotism and the onslaught of majorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The framers sought a government 'strong enough to defend the country... and afford sufficient guarantees to the rights of private property' yet safeguarded against despotism and majority abuses through institutional design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural_secrecy_and_delegate_discretion_in_foundational_conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: In circumstances judged exigent, delegates may set aside narrow instructions, exercise broad discretion, and conduct proceedings in secrecy to avoid premature public interference with the drafting process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delegates 'threw off the restrictions' in their instructions, sat behind closed doors, forbade correspondence on topics under discussion, and deliberately provided for less-than-unanimous ratification — a procedural choice justified by the perceived emergency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration_of_property_qualifications_and_delegation_to_states_when_divided
rubrics_metrics.description: Property qualifications for voters and officers were a considered option to secure class influence, but where consensus failed such matters could be left to state discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Various projects for property qualifications were proposed and defeated due to diversity of opinion; the convention often deferred to the states on contentious items when agreement was impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assemble_experienced_practitioners_for_effective_constitution_making
rubrics_metrics.description: An effective constitutional convention benefits from delegates rich in political experience, practical knowledge, and expertise in law, finance, and administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text praises the Philadelphia assembly as unusually 'rich in political experience' (Washington, Franklin, Hamilton, Madison, etc.), suggesting that such composition contributed to the survival and practical effectiveness of the resulting instrument.
